sec.title: Question
sec.p: Is gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) receptor agonist androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) for prostate cancer associated with accelerated coronary atherosclerosis?

sec.title: Findings
sec.p: In a randomized clinical trial of men with prostate cancer treated with radiotherapy and concomitant ADT, the GnRH agonist leuprolide was associated with a significant increase in 12-month coronary artery total plaque volume of 68.9 mm3 and noncalcified plaque volume of 64.5 mm3 more than treatment with the GnRH antagonist relugolix.

sec.title: Meaning
sec.p: For men with prostate cancer, GnRH agonist leuprolide results in significantly greater near-term coronary plaque progression compared with GnRH antagonist relugolix.

sec.title: Importance
sec.p: Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) for men with prostate cancer (PCa) is associated with cardiovascular (CV) morbidity, yet the biological basis remains unclear. Recent studies have yielded conflicting results regarding the CV safety of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists vs antagonists.

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: To test the hypothesis that ADT is associated with accelerated coronary atherosclerosis and is more prominent with a GnRH agonist compared with a GnRH antagonist.

sec.title: Design, Setting, and Participants
sec.p: This open-label randomized clinical trial was conducted at 4 centers affiliated with a single academic institution in Atlanta, Georgia. Participants were men with nonmetastatic PCa without prior ADT exposure receiving pelvic radiotherapy with ADT of 6 months duration or longer. Patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to either the GnRH agonist leuprolide or the GnRH antagonist relugolix. Trial enrollment was completed between June 16, 2022, and March 6, 2024. Data analysis was completed between March 31, 2025, and June 23, 2025.

sec.title: Intervention
sec.p: Pelvic radiotherapy plus either GnRH agonist leuprolide or GnRH antagonist relugolix.

sec.title: Main Outcomes and Measures
sec.p: The primary end point was change in coronary artery total plaque volume (TPV), measured by coronary computed tomographic angiography completed at baseline and 12 months after ADT initiation. The secondary end point was change in coronary artery noncalcified plaque volume (NCPV). Other outcome measures included change in calcified plaque volume (CPV) and low-attenuation plaque volume (LAPV).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Of 65 men enrolled, 62 (31 in each arm) completed all study procedures for analysis. Mean (SD) age was 68.5 (8.5) years, and 35 of 62 participants (56%) were taking statins. Compared with relugolix, leuprolide was associated with a significantly greater 12-month increase in TPV (estimated difference, +68.9 mm3; 95% CI, 23.2-114.5 mm3; P = .02) and NCPV (+64.5 mm3; 95% CI, 31.6-97.3 mm3; P = .004) after adjustment for baseline plaque volume, age, and statin use. There was no significant difference in 12-month change in CPV or LAPV between patients treated with leuprolide vs relugolix.

sec.title: Conclusions and Relevance
sec.p: In this randomized clinical trial in men with localized PCa treated with radiation plus ADT, the GnRH agonist leuprolide was associated with greater coronary plaque progression within 12 months compared with the GnRH antagonist relugolix. This change was driven by an increase in noncalcified plaque volume and may be mediating ADT-associated CV risk.

abstract.p: This randomized clinical trial tests the hypothesis that androgen deprivation therapy is associated with accelerated coronary atherosclerosis and is more prominent with a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist vs an antagonist.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) targeting the gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) pathway is a cornerstone treatment for prostate cancer (PCa). Injectable GnRH receptor agonists, such as leuprolide, are the most prescribed form.1 However, GnRH agonists have been associated with significant cardiovascular (CV) morbidity, and CV disease is now the leading cause of death in men with PCa.2,3 A first-in-class oral GnRH antagonist, relugolix, was approved in 2020 based on the results of the HERO trial, which demonstrated superior testosterone suppression compared with the GnRH agonist leuprolide. Importantly, after 48 weeks of treatment, there was a 54% lower risk of major adverse CV events (MACE) with relugolix compared with leuprolide.4

The mechanism by which GnRH agonists may increase the near-term risk of MACE, more so than other forms of testosterone suppression, is unclear. The REVELUTION (Relugolix versus Leuprolide Cardiac Trial) randomized clinical trial was designed to test the hypothesis that ADT-associated CV risk is mediated by accelerated coronary atherosclerosis, assessed by prospective coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA), and is more prominent with the GnRH agonist leuprolide compared with the GnRH antagonist relugolix.

sec.title: Trial Design
sec.p: REVELUTION is an open-label randomized clinical trial of men aged 18 years or older with nonmetastatic PCa receiving pelvic radiotherapy (RT) with ADT conducted across 4 centers affiliated with a single institution in Atlanta, Georgia. Patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive relugolix (120 mg taken orally once daily after a single loading dose of 360 mg) or leuprolide acetate (22.5 mg by injection every 3 months). Randomization was stratified according to Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease 10-year risk score. Details regarding participant selection and RT delivery are included in the eMethods in Supplement 2. The trial protocol is available in Supplement 1. This study follows the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) reporting guidelines. The trial was approved by the institutional review board through Emory University in Atlanta, Georgia, registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05320406), and conducted in accordance with the requirements of the regulatory authorities and with the provisions of the Declaration of Helsinki. All patients provided written informed consent.

sec.title: Assessments
sec.p: The primary end point was 12-month change in total plaque volume (TPV), and the secondary end point was change in noncalcified plaque volume (NCPV). Exploratory outcomes were change in calcified plaque volume (CPV) and low-attenuation plaque volume (LAPV). Plaque volume was assessed by serial CCTA completed at baseline (ie, ≤7 days prior to treatment initiation) and 12 months after treatment initiation. All images were acquired on a single 320-slice Canon Aquilion One/GENESIS scanner (Canon Medical Systems) in accordance with clinical guidelines.5 Additional details regarding CCTA are included in the eMethods in Supplement 2.

All CCTA studies were blinded to treatment arm and analyzed using an artificial intelligence–enabled quantitative coronary plaque analysis (AI-QCPA) through a commercially available and validated software (HeartFlow Inc).6 Details regarding AI-QCPA are included in the eMethods in Supplement 2.

Total testosterone concentration level, measured prospectively on serum samples, was measured with a validated liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry method sensitive to 2 ng/dL. (To convert testosterone from nanograms per deciliter to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 0.0347.)

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: The adjusted mean difference was estimated for the change in plaque volume from baseline to month 12 using analysis of covariance. Multivariable adjustment for age, statin use, and respective baseline plaque volume was performed; the inclusion of baseline plaque volume was determined post hoc after observing possible differences in baseline plaque burden between arms. Details regarding the statistical analytic plan are included in the eMethods in Supplement 2 and the trial protocol in Supplement 1. A 2-sided P = .05 significance threshold was used. All analyses were performed using R version 4.4.2 (R Foundation).

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: Trial enrollment was completed between June 16, 2022, and March 6, 2024. Of 65 men who enrolled, 62 completed a baseline and follow-up CCTA scan (31 in each arm) (Figure). Baseline patient characteristics are shown in Table 1. Mean (SD) age was 68.5 (8.5) years, and 35 of 62 participants (56%) were taking statins.

sec.p: For the primary end point of TPV, treatment with leuprolide compared with relugolix was associated with a significantly greater increase from baseline to month 12 (estimated difference, +68.9 mm3; 95% CI, 23.2-114.5 mm3; P = .02), adjusting for baseline TPV, age, and statin use. For the secondary end point of NCPV, treatment with leuprolide compared with relugolix was associated with a significantly greater increase from baseline to month 12 (estimated difference, +64.5 mm3; 95% CI, 31.6-97.3 mm3; P = .004), adjusting for baseline NCPV, age, and statin use. For the exploratory plaque end points of CPV and LAPV, there was no significant difference in 12-month change between leuprolide and relugolix (Table 2).

sec.title: Testosterone Levels
sec.p: Prospective serum testosterone levels between treatments from baseline to month 6 are shown in eTable 3 in Supplement 2. Testosterone levels declined at month 3 and 6, with no significant differences between leuprolide vs relugolix.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Among men with localized PCa receiving RT plus 6 or more months ADT, the GnRH agonist leuprolide was associated with a greater 12-month increase in total coronary plaque volume compared with the GnRH antagonist relugolix, and this change was driven by an increase in noncalcified plaque. This effect appears unrelated to magnitude of testosterone suppression, as leuprolide and relugolix achieved similar levels of castration. Our data demonstrate that the CV effect of ADT is detectable in the near term, at least partly mediated by coronary artery plaque progression, and is drug pathway–specific independent of testosterone suppression.

Multiple observational studies have shown a higher rate of CV morbidity with GnRH agonists compared with orchiectomy or anti-androgen therapy.7,8,9,10 More recently, the phase 3 HERO trial showed an increased incidence of MACE with leuprolide vs relugolix, which was detectable within 4 weeks after treatment initiation.4 REVELUTION results support the CV risk difference between leuprolide and relugolix observed in HERO. Further, our results support the hypothesis that CV risk from ADT may be driven by accelerated coronary atherosclerosis, which is more prominent with GnRH agonist therapy.

Preclinical models suggest that GnRH activation promotes destabilization of existing vascular plaques, especially less stable plaques with noncalcified, thin caps. Cardiac endothelium and CD3-positive T-cells embedded in atherosclerotic plaque express GnRH receptors, and treatment with GnRH agonists may activate these receptors and stimulate T-cell expansion into pro-inflammatory phenotypes implicated in plaque progression and/or rupture.11,12 This proposed mechanism has not been examined in human patients until now. The most prominent difference was related to an increase of noncalcified plaque following leuprolide, which represents less stable atherosclerotic disease that is highly associated with MACE.13,14

sec.title: Strengths and Limitations
sec.p: REVELUTION is strengthened by a diverse patient enrollment and use of CCTA imaging, which yields similar quantitative results to the criterion standard intravascular ultrasonography.15 Given the possible introduction of bias with an open-label design, quantitative imaging analysis was blinded to treatment arm. There are also important limitations. First, the cohort was accrued from a comorbid population in the Southeast US, and most patients had coronary disease at baseline. These results may not be generalizable to healthier populations with lower baseline CV risk. Second, possible changes in statin dose levels after baseline were not recorded. Third, other clinically relevant biomarkers, such as CCTA high-risk plaque features (eg, positive remodeling index, napkin-ring sign, spotty calcification) or high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, were not measured but would be an important post hoc analysis. Finally, REVELUTION was powered to detect differences in CCTA-based plaque volumes, a surrogate for clinical CV risk; our sample was not large enough to measure and validate the impact of leuprolide vs relugolix on MACE.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this randomized clinical trial in men with localized PCa, treatment with leuprolide compared with relugolix was associated with a significantly greater 12-month increase in coronary artery plaque volume. To our knowledge, this is the first clinical trial to identify a biological basis for CV risk differences observed between ADT drug pathways in men with PCa.
